source_evidence.anchor: opening matrix setting and column notation
source_evidence.observation: On PDF page 2 at the opening matrix-setting anchor, the paper takes A ∈ ℝ^{m×n}, m ≥ n, rank(A) = n, and writes A = (a₁,…,aₙ), Q = (q₁,…,qₙ), and R = (rⱼₖ). It separately describes the exact-arithmetic factorization A = QR with QᵀQ = Iₙ and nonsingular upper-triangular R.
On PDF page 3 at Algorithm 2, the Cholesky-like classical Gram-Schmidt algorithm initializes r₁₁ = ‖a₁‖₂, q₁ = a₁/r₁₁, R₁ = (r₁₁), and Q₁ = (q₁).

On PDF page 3 following Algorithm 2, the paper assumes IEEE floating-point arithmetic and states fl(x+y) = (x+y)(1+δ), |δ| ≤ ε_M, for results in the normalized range. It uses (1+ε_M)^{p(n)} = 1+p(n)ε_M+O(ε_M²) for modest p(n), treating the O(ε_M²) contribution as insignificant.

On PDF page 4 at Theorem 1, Aₖ is the first k columns of A, κ₂(Rₖ) = ‖Rₖ‖₂‖Rₖ⁻¹‖₂, and the computed CGS-P factor is assumed to satisfy c₄(m,k)ε_Mκ₂(Rₖ)² < 1 for every k. The residual conclusion is QₖRₖ−Aₖ = ΔAₖ with ‖ΔAₖ‖₂ ≤ c₁(m,k)‖Aₖ‖₂ε_M, where c₁(m,1) = 1, subject to the theorem's O(ε_M²) qualification.
On PDF page 8 at Lemma 2, for the Algorithm 2 outputs satisfying condition (3), r₁₁ = ‖a₁‖₂(1+δ₁) with |δ₁| ≤ (0.5m+1)ε_M+O(ε_M²).
On PDF page 9 after equations (14)-(15), the proof says that condition (3) makes R nonsingular and hence rₖₖ > 0 for every k; this includes r₁₁ > 0.

contract_plain_english: In the paper's full-column-rank setting, run the Cholesky-like classical Gram-Schmidt Algorithm 2 in IEEE floating-point arithmetic and inherit Theorem 1's leading-block condition. For the first column, the computed normalization admits q₁ = (I+G₁)a₁/r₁₁ with ‖G₁‖₂ ≤ ε_M. Consequently, as an exact algebraic relation between the given input column and the stored computed factors, A₁−Q₁R₁ = a₁−q₁r₁₁ = −G₁a₁, and equation (16) gives ‖A₁−Q₁R₁‖₂ = ‖a₁−q₁r₁₁‖₂ ≤ ‖G₁‖₂‖a₁‖₂ ≤ ε_M‖a₁‖₂. This is the k=1 instance of the theorem's residual estimate because c₁(m,1)=1; equation (16) itself has no displayed higher-order remainder.
